title: Logging and Observability
learning_outcomes: Explain what logging and observability contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: structured logging.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Production reliability includes repeatable builds, correct runtime configuration, secret separation, compatible migrations, health checks, logging, monitoring, and a rollback strategy—not only uploading source files. In this lesson, focus on structured logging; then compare it with request identifiers. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use logging and observability when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Production reliability includes repeatable builds, correct runtime configuration, secret separation, compatible migrations, health checks, logging, monitoring, and a rollback strategy—not only uploading source files. For logging and observability, begin with structured logging. Also distinguish request identifiers; metrics and health checks; error reporting. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Logging and Observability
content_blocks.code:
<?php
function requirePositive(int $value): int { if ($value <= 0) { throw new InvalidArgumentException("Value must be positive"); } return $value; }
try { echo requirePositive(3) . PHP_EOL; } catch (InvalidArgumentException $error) { echo "Invalid" . PHP_EOL; }

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep secrets outside build artifacts, run repeatable checks before rollout, and define health checks and rollback plans.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for logging and observability from top to bottom. Start by identifying structured logging, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.

summary: Logging and Observability is one part of the PHP implementation workflow.
Prefer explicit behavior and testable examples over implicit assumptions.
Keep secrets outside build artifacts, run repeatable checks before rollout, and define health checks and rollback plans.
